disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Vendor-neutral; no affiliation with any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original.

choices: Star schema — central fact table (one row per sale) joined to denormalized dimension tables (product, store, date); optimize for analytic reads, accept dimension redundancy
Fully normalized 3NF — best for analytics
One giant flat table — simplest and fastest always
Star schemas can't handle hierarchies
scenarios.hint: Facts in the middle, dimensions around — which shape serves 'slice sales by product, store, and month'?
scenarios.prompt: What modeling pattern fits the analytics workload?
scenarios.situation: A retailer's analysts slice sales by product, store, and month. The OLTP schema needs 8 joins for one report.
scenarios.title: The 8-join report
scenarios.why: Star schema: fact table at the finest grain (one row per sale line, with measures like amount/qty) surrounded by denormalized dimensions (product with category hierarchy inline, date with month/quarter). Analytics queries become 3-4 simple joins with selective dimension filters. Denormalized dimensions trade storage (cheap) for fewer joins (fast). Snowflake normalizes dimensions further — fewer redundancies, more joins; usually not worth it for analytics.

choices: SCD Type 2 — new row per change with effective dates + current flag; preserves full history for 'as-was' reporting
SCD Type 1 — overwrite; history is expendable
Type 2 means two tables
Dimensions never change
scenarios.hint: 'Show me sales by the region the customer was in at purchase time' — which type keeps that answer correct?
scenarios.prompt: Which SCD type, and what does it preserve?
scenarios.situation: Customers change regions. Finance needs historical reports by the region at time of sale, not current region.
scenarios.title: The moving customer
scenarios.why: SCD Type 2 versions the dimension: each change inserts a new row (new surrogate key, effective_from/to, is_current flag); facts reference the version active at event time. Reports then slice by historical truth. Type 1 overwrites (only current truth — history rewrites itself, wrong for compliance). Type 3 keeps one previous value (limited). Choose by the question: 'as-was' → Type 2.

choices: The grain must be declared first (e.g., one row per order line) — every measure and dimension must be consistent with it; mixed grains cause double-counting
Grain doesn't matter as long as joins work
Finer grain is always better regardless of questions
Facts can't have dimensions
scenarios.hint: If one row = one order line, what does SUM(amount) mean — and what breaks if a row sometimes = one order?
scenarios.prompt: Why is grain the first modeling decision?
scenarios.situation: A fact table mixes order headers and order lines. Revenue reports double-count intermittently.
scenarios.title: The grain confusion
scenarios.why: Grain = what one row represents. All measures must be additive at that grain; all dimensions must attach at that grain. Mixed grains (headers + lines in one table) make aggregates meaningless — SUM counts headers and lines together. Declare the grain ('one row per order line'), enforce it in the load, and build separate fact tables for different grains (orders vs lines) rather than mixing.

choices: Junk dimension — combine low-cardinality flags into one dimension table instead of widening the fact; degenerate dimensions (like order number) live directly on the fact
Add 20 flag columns to the fact table
Flags don't need modeling
Create 20 separate dimension tables
scenarios.hint: Where do you put ten yes/no flags without bloating the fact table?
scenarios.prompt: How do you model a pile of low-cardinality flags?
scenarios.situation: Orders carry 12 boolean flags (gift wrap, expedited, international...). The fact table is widening and queries filter on flag combos.
scenarios.title: The flag pile
scenarios.why: Junk dimension: one table with a row per observed flag combination, referenced by a single surrogate key — 12 flags become 1 key, and combo filters become dimension lookups. Degenerate dimensions (transaction numbers, order IDs with no attributes) stay as plain columns on the fact — they're dimensional but need no table. Both keep the fact narrow while preserving analytic power.

choices: Conformed dimensions — shared dimension tables (one date dim, one customer dim) used across fact tables, enabling cross-fact analysis
Each fact gets its own copy of every dimension
Conformed means identical column names only
Sharing dimensions is impossible
scenarios.hint: How do you compare 'sales by month' with 'support tickets by month' on the same month definition?
scenarios.prompt: What enables analysis across multiple fact tables?
scenarios.situation: Sales facts and support-ticket facts each have their own date and customer dimensions with different keys and definitions. Cross-analysis is impossible.
scenarios.title: The two truths
scenarios.why: Conformed dimensions are shared, consistent dimensions across facts: one date dimension, one customer dimension, same keys and definitions everywhere. Then 'sales vs tickets by month' just works. Without them, every mart reinvents 'customer' and numbers never reconcile. Building conformed dimensions is the core data-warehouse discipline — it's what turns marts into a warehouse.

choices: Bridge table (many-to-many) — fact to bridge to dimension; the bridge carries weighting factors so allocations don't double-count
Many-to-many can't be modeled in a star
Put multiple dimension keys in one fact column
Denormalize the dimension into the fact
scenarios.hint: A sale credited to 3 salespeople — how many fact rows, and how do you split the credit?
scenarios.prompt: How do you model a many-to-many fact-dimension relationship?
scenarios.situation: Each sale can involve multiple salespeople with split commission. The star schema assumes one salesperson per sale.
scenarios.title: The split commission
scenarios.why: Bridge table: fact → bridge (one row per fact-dimension pair with an allocation weight, e.g., 0.5/0.3/0.2) → salesperson dimension. Weighted measures (amount × weight) keep totals correct. Without the bridge you'd either duplicate fact rows (double-counting) or lose the split. Multi-valued dimensions are the standard exception to 'one key per dimension'.

choices: ELT — load raw into the warehouse/lake first, then transform with its compute (SQL/dbt); ETL transforms before loading, better when the target is weak or data must be cleansed pre-load
ETL is always better — transforming early is cleaner
ELT means no transformation happens
The order doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: If your target is a warehouse with massive SQL compute, where should the heavy transform run?
scenarios.prompt: When does ELT beat ETL?
scenarios.situation: A team with a cloud warehouse runs ETL: transforms in Python on small VMs, then loads. Transforms are slow and the warehouse sits idle.
scenarios.title: The idle warehouse
scenarios.why: ELT loads raw data first, then transforms inside the warehouse using its elastic SQL compute (dbt models, SQL transforms) — the transform scales with the platform built for it. ETL (transform-then-load) fits when: the target can't transform (a dashboard DB), data must be cleansed/masked before landing (compliance), or bandwidth forces reduction at the edge. Match the pattern to where compute lives.

choices: Idempotent loads — MERGE/upsert on natural keys, or delete+insert partitions by watermark; reruns produce identical results
Reruns should be avoided rather than made safe
Idempotency requires exactly-once infrastructure
Overwrite the whole table every time — simplest
scenarios.hint: What property makes 'just rerun it' a safe incident response?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a pipeline rerunnable without corruption?
scenarios.situation: A daily load fails halfway. Rerunning it duplicates half the day's rows.
scenarios.title: The half-loaded day
scenarios.why: Idempotent loads: rerunning yields the same result as running once. Patterns: MERGE/upsert keyed on natural keys; partition overwrite (delete the day's partition, rewrite it); staging + atomic swap. Non-idempotent appends duplicate on retry — the classic pipeline corruption. Design every load so the incident response can be 'rerun it' instead of 'surgically repair it'.

choices: Change data capture — read the database's transaction log (or use Debezium-style connectors) for row-level inserts/updates/deletes in near real time
Full table scans hourly — simplest and complete
CDC can't capture deletes
Triggers on every table — cleanest
scenarios.hint: Where is every committed change already recorded, in order?
scenarios.prompt: How do you stream database changes without hammering the source?
scenarios.situation: An orders database must feed the warehouse with minute-level freshness, including deletes. Hourly full scans crush the OLTP database.
scenarios.title: The chatty source
scenarios.why: CDC tails the database transaction log — every insert/update/delete, in commit order, with minimal source impact (log reading, not querying). It captures deletes (as delete events) which 'updated_at > watermark' polling misses. Full scans don't scale; triggers add OLTP overhead. CDC is the standard for operational-to-analytical sync.

choices: Schema evolution strategy — backward-compatible changes (add nullable columns) flow through; breaking changes (renames, type changes) need versioned contracts and migration; use schema registries for streams
Ignore schema changes; pipelines adapt automatically
Breaking changes are fine if documented in chat
Freeze all schemas forever
scenarios.hint: Which changes break downstream consumers, and which are safe?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle upstream schema changes?
scenarios.situation: A source team renames user_id → customer_id. Three pipelines break silently (NULL joins) before anyone notices.
scenarios.title: The renamed column
scenarios.why: Classify changes: additive/nullable = backward compatible (old consumers unaffected); renames/type changes/deletions = breaking. Defenses: schema registry with compatibility checks (BACKWARD/FORWARD/FULL) for streams; data contracts between producers and consumers; column-level lineage to find affected pipelines; tests asserting expected schema on load. Silent renames are pipeline killers — make them loud.

choices: Watermark-based incremental loads — track max(updated_at) or an incrementing id; handle late/out-of-order data with a lookback window
Full reloads daily — simplest correct
Watermarks guarantee completeness
Timestamps are always reliable
scenarios.hint: If events can arrive late, what does 'everything after the watermark' miss?
scenarios.prompt: How do incremental loads work, and what is the late-data caveat?
scenarios.situation: An incremental job loads rows with updated_at > last watermark. Late-arriving events (backdated corrections) are missed.
scenarios.title: The watermark gap
scenarios.why: Watermarks (high-water marks on updated_at or sequential ids) load only new/changed rows — efficient. But 'greater than watermark' assumes event time ≈ arrival time. Late/backdated data needs a lookback window (reprocess last N hours/days) or CDC. Also: updated_at must be reliably maintained by the source (no bulk updates without timestamp bumps), or rows silently skip.

choices: Staging + atomic swap (or partition exchange) — load into staging, validate, then swap into production in one atomic operation; readers never see partial data
Load directly into production tables — fastest
Readers can handle partial data
Staging doubles storage permanently
scenarios.hint: How do you make a 2-hour load appear instantaneously to readers?
scenarios.prompt: How do you publish a rebuilt table without downtime or partial reads?
scenarios.situation: A 2-hour full rebuild of a reporting table leaves dashboards showing partial data mid-load.
scenarios.title: The partial dashboard
scenarios.why: Load into a staging table (or new partition), run validation checks, then atomically swap (ALTER TABLE ... SWITCH partition, or rename swap) — readers flip from old-complete to new-complete with no partial state. Direct loads expose intermediate states. The pattern costs temporary staging space and buys correctness; it's the standard for full-refresh publishes.

choices: Lakehouse (Delta Lake/Iceberg/Hudi on the lake) — open formats + ACID transactions + schema enforcement + time travel, without moving off cheap object storage
A traditional warehouse — lakes can't do transactions
Plain Parquet files — they have ACID already
Lakehouses are just marketing; keep CSVs
scenarios.hint: What adds transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel to Parquet files on object storage?
scenarios.prompt: What architecture gives warehouse guarantees on a data lake?
scenarios.situation: A data lake of Parquet files has no transactions, no schema enforcement, and readers see partial writes. The team debates moving to a warehouse.
scenarios.title: The lake with no guarantees
scenarios.why: Lakehouse table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) layer ACID transactions, schema enforcement/evolution, and time travel over Parquet/ORC files on object storage — warehouse reliability at lake storage cost. Concurrent writers get isolation; readers get snapshots. It's the answer to 'lake chaos vs warehouse cost' for most analytics.

choices: Parquet (columnar) — analytic queries read few columns over many rows; columnar layout + compression + predicate pushdown crush row formats on scans
CSV — human-readable and universal
JSON — flexible and fast for analytics
Row formats are better for aggregations
scenarios.hint: A query reads 3 of 50 columns — which layout skips the other 47?
scenarios.prompt: Why is Parquet the analytic standard?
scenarios.situation: A lake stores CSVs. A query scanning 1 TB to aggregate 2 columns takes forever and costs a fortune.
scenarios.title: The CSV lake
scenarios.why: Parquet is columnar: values of one column are stored together — compressed (same-type data compresses well), with min/max statistics per row group enabling predicate pushdown (skip whole row groups). A 2-column aggregation reads ~4% of the data instead of 100%. CSV/JSON are row-oriented: every query reads everything. Format choice is a 10-25x cost/performance lever.

choices: Partition by the filter columns queries actually use (e.g., date), with partition sizes in the hundreds of MB — too many small partitions = metadata overhead and slow listing
Partition by every column — maximum pruning
Partition by a high-cardinality id — even distribution
Partitioning doesn't matter with Parquet
scenarios.hint: 10M tiny partitions vs 100 well-sized ones — which lists faster and prunes better?
scenarios.prompt: What is the partitioning discipline?
scenarios.situation: A table partitioned by hour has 50k tiny partitions. Queries listing partitions time out; the metastore groans.
scenarios.title: The partition explosion
scenarios.why: Partitioning prunes data (skip irrelevant date partitions), but each partition is metadata + files. Too fine (hourly for small data, or high-cardinality keys) → small-files problem: slow listings, metastore bloat, poor compression. Discipline: partition by common filter columns (usually date), target ~100 MB–1 GB per partition/file, compact small files (OPTIMIZE/VACUUM in lakehouse formats). Partition for pruning, not for sharding.

choices: Medallion (bronze/silver/gold) — bronze: raw ingested; silver: cleaned/conformed; gold: business-level aggregates; each layer has a contract and owner
One layer is enough — transformations can happen in BI
Medallion means three databases
Silver is optional
scenarios.hint: Raw landing, cleaned entities, business aggregates — which layer does each belong to?
scenarios.prompt: What is the medallion pattern, and what does each layer guarantee?
scenarios.situation: Analysts query raw ingestion tables directly; every dashboard reimplements the same cleaning logic differently.
scenarios.title: The raw-table free-for-all
scenarios.why: Medallion layers: Bronze = raw, immutable landing (replayable source of truth); Silver = cleaned, deduplicated, conformed entities (the 'one true' customer/order); Gold = aggregated, business-ready marts (KPIs, dashboard tables). Contracts: analysts build on gold/silver, never bronze; each layer is validated. It ends the 'every dashboard cleans differently' chaos.

choices: Serve the query pattern: warehouse/lakehouse for SQL analytics, with caching/aggregates or a serving store (key-value/search) for low-latency app reads — don't serve apps directly from the warehouse
Serve everything from the warehouse — it's the single source of truth
Copy the warehouse to the app database nightly — freshness doesn't matter
Apps should query Parquet files directly
scenarios.hint: A dashboard needing p99 < 200ms — is a warehouse scan the right serving path?
scenarios.prompt: How do you serve different latency needs from one platform?
scenarios.situation: An app needs sub-second lookups of user features; analysts need ad-hoc SQL over billions of rows. One warehouse serves both badly.
scenarios.title: The serving split
scenarios.why: Warehouses optimize for throughput over billions of rows, not millisecond point lookups. Pattern: warehouse/lakehouse as the analytical backbone + a serving layer for operational reads (materialized aggregates, caches, key-value or search stores fed by pipelines). Match serving tech to the SLA: SQL analytics → warehouse; live app reads → serving store. One engine rarely serves both well.

choices: Time travel — query the table as of a timestamp/version for audits, debugging, and rollback; retention settings bound how far back you can go
Time travel is only for backups
You need a separate audit table
Snapshots are manual only
evidence:
SELECT * FROM orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-10-01 09:00:00';
-- or VERSION AS OF 42
scenarios.hint: The bad load ran at 10 AM — how do you see the table as of 9 AM without restoring anything?
scenarios.prompt: How do you recover from a bad load without a restore?
scenarios.situation: A buggy transform corrupts the gold orders table at 10 AM. The team debates restoring from yesterday's backup (losing today's good data).
scenarios.title: The bad load
scenarios.why: Lakehouse time travel queries historical snapshots (TIMESTAMP/VERSION AS OF) — inspect the 9 AM state, diff against now, and either roll back (RESTORE) or surgically fix. No backup restore, no data loss window beyond the bad writes. Retention (e.g., 30 days of history) bounds the lookback. It's also the audit answer: 'what did this metric show last Tuesday?'

choices: Event time (when it happened) vs processing time (when the system saw it) — windowing and correctness use event time; watermarks bound how long you wait for late events
They are the same thing
Processing time is always correct
Event time can't be trusted
scenarios.hint: A phone offline for 2 hours uploads events — which 'time' puts them in the right hour?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the distinction matter?
scenarios.situation: Mobile events arrive hours late (offline phones). Hourly counts by arrival time misattribute them.
scenarios.title: The late phone
scenarios.why: Event time = when the event occurred (the business truth); processing time = when the pipeline saw it (an accident of connectivity). Correct windows use event time; watermarks ('we've seen all events up to T, modulo lateness') let the system close windows while tolerating late data. Late events past the watermark go to a side output or are dropped by policy — a business decision, not a bug.

choices: Tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping: hourly counts), sliding (overlapping: 5-min avg every minute), session (activity-based gaps) — match the window to the question
All windows are the same
Tumbling windows overlap
Session windows have fixed sizes
scenarios.hint: 'Count per hour' vs '5-minute average updated every minute' vs 'user sessions' — which window each?
scenarios.prompt: How do the window types differ?
scenarios.situation: Three metrics: hourly order counts, a 5-min moving average refreshed every minute, and user session durations.
scenarios.title: The three windows
scenarios.why: Tumbling: fixed non-overlapping (each event in exactly one hour bucket) — for per-period counts. Sliding: fixed size, sliding interval (5-min window every 1 min) — for moving averages. Session: dynamic, bounded by inactivity gaps — for behavior sessions. Choosing wrong gives wrong answers: sliding for 'per hour' double-counts; tumbling for sessions splits behavior arbitrarily.

choices: Exactly-once = idempotent sinks + transactional/checkpointed state (e.g., Kafka transactions + idempotent producers); at-least-once duplicates on retry, at-most-once loses on failure
Exactly-once means the source sends once
At-least-once is the same as exactly-once
Semantics don't matter for analytics
scenarios.hint: If the network retries a write, what prevents the duplicate — the transport, or the sink?
scenarios.prompt: What does exactly-once actually require?
scenarios.situation: A billing stream double-charges on retries. The team assumed 'Kafka is exactly-once' by default.
scenarios.title: The double charge
scenarios.why: Exactly-once is end-to-end: idempotent producers + transactions (Kafka) or checkpointed state + idempotent sinks (Flink). At-least-once (retry on failure) duplicates; at-most-once (no retry) loses. Nothing is exactly-once 'by default' — the sink must dedupe (idempotent keys) or participate in transactions. For money: exactly-once or idempotent sink; for metrics: at-least-once is fine.

choices: Lambda (batch + speed layers, merged at serving) vs Kappa (single stream processor, replay for batch) — kappa simplifies to one codebase when the stream processor can replay history
Lambda is always better
Kappa can't do batch
They are identical
scenarios.hint: Do you maintain two codebases (batch + streaming) or one that replays?
scenarios.prompt: What is the architectural trade-off?
scenarios.situation: A team maintains Spark batch jobs and a separate Flink streaming job computing the same metrics — logic drifts between them.
scenarios.title: The two codebases
scenarios.why: Lambda: batch layer (accurate, high latency) + speed layer (approximate, low latency), merged at query time — two systems to maintain, logic drift risk. Kappa: one stream processor handles everything; 'batch' = replaying the log from the start. Kappa wins when the log is replayable and the stream engine handles historical scale; lambda persists where batch tooling is deeply entrenched. The drift they feel is lambda's core cost.

choices: Backpressure handling — bounded queues, load shedding, or autoscaling consumers; monitor consumer lag as the key health metric
Add more partitions blindly
Backpressure means the system is broken
Lag is unmeasurable
scenarios.hint: Producers outrun consumers 10:1 — what absorbs the spike, and what metric proves it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you survive a traffic spike?
scenarios.situation: A flash sale produces 10x normal events. Consumers fall behind; the queue grows unbounded and OOMs.
scenarios.title: The flash-sale spike
scenarios.why: Streams must handle producer/consumer speed mismatch: the log buffers the spike (that's its job), consumers scale horizontally, and consumer lag (offset behind head) is the health metric to alert on. Without bounds: shed load (drop low-priority events by policy), scale consumers, or degrade gracefully. Unbounded buffering just moves the OOM around. Design for the spike, not the average.

choices: Event-driven micro-batch or true streaming when freshness < minutes is worth the complexity; otherwise scheduled batch — don't pay streaming's operational cost for a daily report
Streaming is always better
Batch is obsolete
Freshness requirements don't affect architecture
scenarios.hint: Does anyone act on this data within minutes? If not, what are you buying with streaming?
scenarios.prompt: How do you decide?
scenarios.situation: A team builds a Flink pipeline for a daily executive report 'because streaming is modern'. It pages on-call weekly.
scenarios.title: The streaming hammer
scenarios.why: Streaming buys freshness at the cost of operational complexity (state management, watermarks, exactly-once, 24/7 on-call). If the decision latency is hours/days, batch is simpler, cheaper, and more debuggable. Rule: let the required freshness (minutes? hours?) choose the architecture. 'Modern' is not a requirement; the SLA is.

choices: DAG (directed acyclic graph) — tasks with declared dependencies, no cycles; the scheduler runs tasks when upstreams succeed, with retries and alerting
Cron jobs with sleep statements between them
DAGs can have cycles
Dependencies are documentation only
scenarios.hint: What breaks when job B starts before job A finishes, and how do declared dependencies fix it?
scenarios.prompt: Why orchestrate with DAGs instead of cron chains?
scenarios.situation: Five cron jobs chained by timing estimates. When job 2 runs long, job 3 processes partial data.
scenarios.title: The cron chain
scenarios.why: A DAG declares dependencies explicitly: task B runs when task A succeeds (not when the clock says A 'should' be done). The orchestrator handles retries, backfills, alerting, and visibility. Cron chains encode dependencies as time guesses — fragile under variance. Acyclicity matters: cycles = deadlock. Orchestration turns 'hope the timing works' into 'guaranteed ordering'.

choices: Idempotent tasks + retry with backoff on transient failures; retries of non-idempotent tasks corrupt data — make tasks rerunnable first
Retry everything blindly — retries are always safe
Never retry; fail loudly
Retries replace idempotency
scenarios.hint: What happens when the retry of a half-finished append runs?
scenarios.prompt: What is the retry discipline?
scenarios.situation: A task fails after writing half its output. The retry appends again — duplicates.
scenarios.title: The retry that duplicated
scenarios.why: Retries are safe only for idempotent tasks (rerun = same result). Retry policy: transient errors (network blips, throttling) → retry with exponential backoff + jitter; permanent errors (bad SQL, schema mismatch) → fail fast and alert. Retry budgets cap the blast radius. The order matters: make tasks idempotent first, then retries become a reliability feature instead of a corruption vector.

choices: Backfill as a first-class operation — the orchestrator reruns the DAG over the date range with the same code; ensure idempotent loads so reruns are safe
Manually run scripts for missing days
Backfills aren't needed if monitoring is good
Rerun the whole history every time
scenarios.hint: The code is fixed — now how do you recompute March 3–5 with it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you recompute a date range after a bug?
scenarios.situation: A bug corrupted March 3–5 outputs. The fix is deployed; now the bad days must be recomputed.
scenarios.title: The bad week
scenarios.why: Backfill = rerun the DAG for a date range with corrected code. Requirements: parameterized runs (execution date, not 'today'), idempotent writes (partition overwrite/MERGE), and enough history (bronze layer!) to recompute from. Catchup (running missed schedules on deploy) is the related concept — decide explicitly whether deploys backfill or skip. Without backfill capability, every bug is permanent.

choices: Sensors / data-aware scheduling — trigger when the upstream data lands (file sensor, table sensor), not at a fixed time; decouples teams' schedules
Fixed cron times — simplest coordination
Sensors poll forever with no timeout
Upstream teams should just be faster
scenarios.hint: Upstream lands at 2 AM some days, 5 AM others — what triggers downstream correctly both days?
scenarios.prompt: How do you coordinate across teams' pipelines?
scenarios.situation: Downstream runs at 3 AM daily; upstream lands between 2–5 AM. Downstream often processes yesterday's data or fails.
scenarios.title: The 3 AM gamble
scenarios.why: Time-based triggers assume upstream punctuality — wrong. Sensors wait for the data condition (file present, partition committed, table updated) with timeouts and SLAs. Data-aware scheduling decouples teams: upstream owns 'data lands by SLA', downstream owns 'process when it lands'. Fixed-time chains across teams are the #1 cross-team pipeline failure.

choices: SLA + alerting on task/DAG duration and data freshness (not just success) — a 'successful' 6-hour-late DAG is a failure; page on SLA miss, notify on retry storms
Alert only on task failure
Success means on time
Freshness can't be monitored
scenarios.hint: The DAG succeeded — 8 hours late. Did your alerting notice?
scenarios.prompt: What do you alert on besides failure?
scenarios.situation: A DAG 'succeeds' daily but finishes at noon instead of 6 AM. Nobody is alerted; stakeholders complain.
scenarios.title: The late success
scenarios.why: Pipeline health = correctness + freshness. Alert on: task/DAG failure, SLA miss (duration over expected), data freshness (downstream tables' max timestamp vs now), and data quality checks (row counts, null rates). A green DAG that's 6 hours late is a silent SLA breach. Monitor the data's arrival, not just the task's exit code.

choices: Branching + conditional tasks (or dynamic task mapping) — the DAG structure adapts to the data; keep the graph readable and test the branches
One DAG per variant — simplest
Dynamic DAGs can't be tested
Branching makes lineage impossible
scenarios.hint: 10 regions need the same pipeline with different parameters — one DAG or ten?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle pipelines that vary by input?
scenarios.situation: A pipeline runs per region (10 regions) with slight parameter differences. Ten copy-pasted DAGs drift apart.
scenarios.title: The ten DAGs
scenarios.why: Parameterize: one DAG template × parameters (dynamic task mapping / config-driven DAGs) instead of copy-paste. Branching handles conditional logic (skip region with no data). Benefits: one codebase, consistent logic, per-region observability via mapped task instances. Keep dynamic generation deterministic and testable — generated-at-parse-time surprises are the failure mode.

choices: Tests at every stage: schema conformance, row-count/volume bounds, null-rate and uniqueness checks, freshness SLAs — fail the pipeline (or quarantine) on violation, don't silently pass bad data
Manual spot checks weekly
Tests slow pipelines down too much
Quality is the analyst's job
scenarios.hint: If the check runs after the dashboard refreshes, what did it protect?
scenarios.prompt: What does a data-test suite look like?
scenarios.situation: A source drops a column; dashboards show NULLs for a week before anyone notices.
scenarios.title: The silent NULLs
scenarios.why: Data tests run inside the pipeline: schema tests (expected columns/types), volume tests (row count within bounds — catches partial loads), distribution tests (null rates, distinct counts), freshness tests (max timestamp recency). On failure: halt or quarantine the batch (don't publish bad data downstream), alert with context. Tests belong before publication — a check after the dashboard refreshes is an autopsy.

choices: Data contracts — producer and consumer agree on schema, semantics, SLAs, and change policy; versioned and enforced (schema registry, CI checks)
Contracts are bureaucracy; move fast
Verbal agreements are sufficient
Contracts can't be enforced technically
scenarios.hint: Who decides what 'active user' means — the producer, or each consumer separately?
scenarios.prompt: How do you prevent upstream changes from breaking downstream?
scenarios.situation: Three teams define 'revenue' differently; the CEO's dashboard disagrees with finance. Upstream renames break pipelines monthly.
scenarios.title: The three revenues
scenarios.why: A data contract is the API of data: schema, semantics ('revenue = recognized, net of refunds'), quality SLAs, and change policy (how breaking changes are announced/versioned). Enforced via schema registries, CI checks on producers, and consumer tests. It moves the agreement from tribal knowledge to a versioned artifact — the fix for both 'three definitions' and 'surprise renames'.

choices: Column-level lineage — track every column from source to dashboard; when the source changes, the lineage graph names every affected pipeline and report
Lineage is documentation; grep is enough
Table-level lineage is sufficient for impact analysis
Lineage can't be automated
scenarios.hint: The source column is renamed — how do you find all 40 downstream usages without reading every pipeline?
scenarios.prompt: What does lineage buy you operationally?
scenarios.situation: A deprecated source column feeds 40 downstream assets. The migration team must find them all.
scenarios.title: The column deprecation
scenarios.why: Lineage (ideally column-level, captured automatically from pipeline code/SQL parsing) answers: 'what breaks if I change X?' and 'why is this dashboard wrong?' (trace back to the source). It's the impact-analysis tool for migrations, the debugging tool for incidents, and the auditor's evidence for compliance. Manual lineage docs rot; automated capture from code is the sustainable path.

choices: Classify, minimize, and protect: tag PII at ingestion, mask/tokenize in non-prod and for unauthorized roles, enforce access controls, and honor deletion requests through the pipeline (including backups)
PII handling is the app's problem, not the pipeline's
Masking destroys data utility entirely
Deletion requests only apply to production tables
scenarios.hint: A developer copies prod to a laptop for debugging — which controls should have made that useless or impossible?
scenarios.prompt: How do pipelines handle PII responsibly?
scenarios.situation: Analytics needs user behavior data; privacy requires that raw emails never reach analysts or dev environments.
scenarios.title: The PII pipeline
scenarios.why: Pipeline PII discipline: classify at ingestion (tag PII columns), mask/tokenize for analytics and non-prod (analysts get hashed IDs, not emails), enforce column-level access, and design for deletion (right-to-erasure must propagate through bronze→gold and backups — hard with immutable logs, so minimize PII upstream). Privacy isn't a downstream filter; it's an architectural property of the pipeline.

choices: Freshness + completeness + validity SLAs per dataset, with error budgets and clear ownership — 'data downtime' measured like system downtime
SLAs are only for APIs
100% freshness is achievable
Ownership can stay vague
scenarios.hint: If the dashboard is stale, who gets paged — and what does 'stale' mean in minutes?
scenarios.prompt: How do you define reliability for data?
scenarios.situation: Stakeholders assume dashboards are real-time; the pipeline is daily. Every 'delay' becomes an escalation.
scenarios.title: The freshness argument
scenarios.why: Data SLAs make reliability explicit: freshness (data no older than X), completeness (all sources landed), validity (quality checks pass) — per dataset, with an owner who gets paged. 'Data downtime' = periods the data isn't usable, measured like uptime. Without SLAs, every delay is a surprise; with them, expectations are set and breaches are managed, not escalated.

choices: Quarantine pattern — bad batches go to a quarantine area with diagnostics; pipeline halts or skips per policy; never silently publish bad data or silently drop it
Silently drop bad rows — cleanest output
Publish everything; consumers filter
Quarantine is the same as deleting
scenarios.hint: The batch fails validation — do you publish it, drop it, or put it somewhere for investigation?
scenarios.prompt: What happens to a batch that fails validation?
scenarios.situation: 5% of rows in a batch violate the schema. Publishing corrupts dashboards; dropping loses data silently.
scenarios.title: The bad batch
scenarios.why: Quarantine: route failing batches/rows to a quarantine zone with full diagnostics (which check failed, sample rows), halt or skip downstream per policy, alert with context. It preserves the evidence for root-causing while protecting consumers. Silent drops hide systemic issues; publishing bad data destroys trust. Quarantine is the third option that keeps both honesty and reliability.
